title: Influence of pairing and correlations on transport properties in three-terminal superconducting nanostructure
authors: G. Górski, V. Pokorný, T. Domański
abstract: We study the local and nonlocal charge transport properties of three-terminal nanostructure, consisting of the correlated quantum dot embedded between two metallic electrodes and superconductor. Using the linear response theory, we analyze interplay of the induced on-dot pairing with the correlation effects, inspecting their influence on the conductance and thermopower. Our calculations predict negative values of the nonlocal conductance and reversal of the Seebeck coefficient when the quantum dot ground state is represented by the BCS-type singlet configuration. These phenomena are realized when the subgap charge transport is predominantly contributed by the crossed Andreev scattering. In contrast, on the doublet side, we obtain signatures for the Kondo effect manifested by the low-temperature enhancement of the charge conductance and clearly evident in the thermopower. Such temperature-dependent local and nonlocal transport properties can unambiguously identify the specific configuration of the correlated quantum dot and reveal the rich physics emerging in the doublet-to-singlet crossover region.
summary: This theoretical work analyzes charge transport in a superconducting nanostructure containing a correlated quantum dot. By applying linear response theory, the authors map out how electron-electron correlations and superconducting pairing manifest in measurable quantities like conductance and thermopower. The results provide a clear diagnostic tool to distinguish between different ground state configurations, such as the BCS singlet state versus the Kondo doublet state.
main_problem: The study investigates how the interplay between induced on-dot pairing (superconductivity) and electron correlation effects influences the local and nonlocal charge transport properties in a three-terminal nanostructure.
main_result: The calculations predict distinct signatures: negative nonlocal conductance and Seebeck coefficient reversal in the BCS singlet state due to crossed Andreev scattering, while the Kondo effect is visible on the doublet side via conductance enhancement.
method: The analysis employs linear response theory, utilizing the Dyson equation framework to calculate transport coefficients by treating correlation effects perturbatively via the self-energy.
model_or_system: The system is a correlated quantum dot (QD) modeled by the Anderson impurity Hamiltonian, coupled to two normal metallic leads and one superconducting electrode. The model incorporates Coulomb repulsion (U) and the superconducting pairing gap (Delta).
key_observables: Local and nonlocal conductance ($G$), thermopower (Seebeck coefficient $S$), and the spectral function $A(\omega)$.
important_parameters: The key regimes include the BCS-type singlet ground state, the Kondo regime (doublet side), and the crossover region between them, controlled by parameters like U, Delta, and temperature T.
main_assumptions: The primary approximation involves treating correlation effects perturbatively via the self-energy, which is assumed reliable for studying the Kondo effect and parity transition.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the spectral function transition from BCS-type peaks to the Kondo Abrikosov-Suhl peak, and diagrams show the phase boundary between singlet and doublet configurations.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the three-terminal setup and the underlying Hamiltonian, progresses through the application of linear response theory to derive transport currents, and concludes by analyzing the specific signatures of the Kondo effect and pairing interactions in the resulting conductance and thermopower.
why_interesting: The interplay between superconductivity (pairing) and strong correlations (Kondo physics) in nanoscale devices is a frontier area in condensed matter physics, directly relevant to understanding superconducting spintronics and quantum transport.
